set.abstract: Disease is one of the fundamental entities in biomedical research. Recognizing such entities from biomedical text and then normalizing them to a standardized disease vocabulary offer a tremendous opportunity for many downstream applications. Previous studies have demonstrated that joint modeling of the two sub-tasks has superior performance than the pipelined counterpart. Although the neural joint model based on multi-task learning framework has achieved state-of-the-art performance, it suffers from the boundary inconsistency problem due to the separate decoding procedures. Moreover, it ignores the rich information (e.g., the text surface form) of each candidate concept in the vocabulary, which is quite essential for entity normalization. In this work, we propose a neural transition-based joint model to alleviate these two issues. We transform the end-to-end disease recognition and normalization task as an action sequence prediction task, which not only jointly learns the model with shared representations of the input, but also jointly searches the output by state transitions in one search space. Moreover, we introduce attention mechanisms to take advantage of the text surface form of each candidate concept for better normalization performance. Experimental results conducted on two publicly available datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

NeuJoRN represents words using a character CNN, GloVe and ELMo, followed by BiLSTM; stack and action history use StackLSTM. OUT, SHIFT, REDUCE and SEGMENT-t support recognition, while LINKING-c supports normalization. Candidate-aware context attention and mention–concept CoAttention inform linking. BERT is explicitly left for future work, not an evaluated backbone.

Inputs are sentences plus a controlled vocabulary, though evaluation includes abstract-level normalization. NCBI is reported as 792 PubMed abstracts, with 692 combined training/development and 100 test; BC5CDR has 1,500 abstracts equally split across training/development/test. Table 3 reports 6,881/12,852 mentions and 1,049/5,818 concepts. These are source-reported corpus statistics, not independently re-counted unique concepts or patient cohorts.

The official NCBI Disease Corpus page, captured on 2026-10-24 and marked revised August 27, 2013, lists 793 PubMed abstracts, 6,892 disease mentions and 790 unique disease concepts. This paper instead reports 792 abstracts, 6,881 mentions and 1,049 concepts in Table 3. Both source statistics are retained. No filtering, deduplication, version or count-definition explanation is established, and the paper’s concepts column is not assumed equivalent to the official unique-concept count. Official source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/CBBresearch/Dogan/DISEASE/.

The study uses the July 6, 2012 MEDIC vocabulary: 7,827 MeSH identifiers and 4,004 OMIM identifiers grouped into 9,664 disease concepts. Spelling correction, Ab3p and Wikipedia-derived abbreviation expansion, and numeric-synonym normalization precede Lucene BM25 retrieval over concept names and training mentions. Only the top 10 concepts are candidate linking actions. Candidate-retrieval recall and open-world vocabulary coverage are not separately reported.

Recognition F1 is evaluated at the mention level; normalization F1 is evaluated at the abstract level using the cited BioCreative evaluation kit. These scores must not be described as per-mention entity-linking accuracy, calibrated clinical confidence or patient-level diagnosis. NIL is defined for unlinkable mentions, but no separate NIL/open-set benchmark is reported.

Table 5 reports NeuJoRN versus MTL-feedback on NCBI recognition/normalization 88.57/88.82 versus 87.43/88.23, and BC5CDR 88.19/89.86 versus 87.62/89.17. The absolute gains are 1.14/0.59 and 0.57/0.69 percentage points, not relative percentages. These are comparisons with the paper’s selected 2021-era baselines, not a current-state-of-the-art claim.

Table 6 evaluates greedy and beam search with beam sizes 1, 2 and 4 only. Beam 4 is best among these tested settings. Greedy uses local negative-log-likelihood training, while beam uses Beam-Search Optimization with LaSO and max-margin loss; the comparison does not isolate search width from objective/training changes. Greedy is below MTL-feedback on all four reported metrics. The stated larger-beam speed tradeoff has no measured runtime/latency table.

Table 7’s complete beam-4 baseline is 88.57/88.82 and 88.19/89.86 on NCBI and BC5CDR recognition/normalization. Removing local-context attention gives 88.27/88.68 and 88.03/89.64; removing CoAttention gives 86.73/87.79 and 87.29/88.53. CoAttention removal has the larger drops in this setting, but the paper gives no confidence intervals, variance, seed counts or identified statistical test; its word “significantly” is not proof of statistical significance.

The proposed joint decoding addresses separate-search boundary inconsistency, but the experiments do not separately quantify boundary-inconsistency error rates or prove all recognition/linking errors are eliminated. Candidate limitations, annotation assumptions and preprocessing remain material dependencies. No clinical efficacy, diagnostic, safety, fairness or prospective deployment study is presented; clinical notes, drug labels and tweets are explicitly future work.
